title: Community Rights and Responsibilities
keyIdea: A right is something every child should have so they can live, grow, learn, be safe and be heard. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) has 54 articles, and 42 of them set out children's rights, such as the right to education and the right to be safe from harm. Rights belong to every child and are not earned by good behaviour, so they cannot be taken away as a punishment; privileges can. Because everyone has the same rights, each of us has a responsibility to respect other people's rights, and adults and governments have a duty to make rights happen.

kid: A right is something every child should have. You need it to live, grow, learn and be safe. Going to school is a right. So is being kept safe from harm.
A want is different. A new phone is nice, but you can live and grow without it. Rights are about needs, not wants.
Rights belong to every child. You do not earn them by being good, and you do not lose them by being naughty. A treat like golden time can be taken away. Food and safety cannot.

Everyone has the same rights as you. So your part is to respect theirs. If you have the right to be heard, you listen when others speak. Grown-ups and the government have a job too: they must make rights happen.
adult: In England, the PSHE Association programme for Key Stage 2 asks pupils to learn that human rights are there to protect everyone, and how rights relate to responsibilities. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted in 1989. The UK ratified it in 1991. It has 54 articles, 42 of which give rights to everyone under 18.

Key words: a right holder is the child. A duty bearer is an adult or body that must make the right happen, such as the government, teachers and other adults working for the state, and parents and carers. Rights are universal and inherent: they cannot be earned, traded or removed. A privilege, such as extra screen time, can be given or withdrawn. Article 12 gives the right to be heard. Article 19 is protection from harm. Article 28 is education, and school discipline must respect the child's dignity.

Common mistakes: saying children must earn their rights, or lose them for bad behaviour. Confusing wants with rights. Thinking a right means always getting your own way. Thinking only children have responsibilities, when adults and governments are the main duty bearers. Be careful with the phrase no rights without responsibilities. UNICEF UK's Rights Respecting Schools guidance warns against it, because rights are unconditional.

In the lab, learners sort rights from wants and match a right to the respect it asks of them. They find which punishments would break a child's rights, settle three everyday clashes on a balance with a fair fix, and hand each right to its duty bearer.

familyTip: When a family rule is broken, talk about what is a privilege (screen time, a treat) and what is a right (food, safety, being listened to). Ask: which ones could we take away, and which ones never?

visual.caption: Right or privilege? Drag each card to a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort rights from wants, mirror a right onto everyone else, find punishments that break rights, balance clashes, and match rights to duty bearers.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a right for every child?
practice.hint: A right is something every child needs to live, grow and be safe.
practice.explain: Clean water and healthy food are rights (Article 24). A bike and a holiday are nice wants.

practice.prompt: A class sorts {a} cards. {b} of them are rights and the rest are wants. How many cards are wants?
practice.hint: Every card is either a right or a want. Take the rights away from the total.

practice.prompt: Leo hit someone. Which consequence is allowed?
choices: Being called names by the teacher
practice.hint: Which one is a privilege, and which ones are rights?
practice.explain: Golden time is a privilege, so it can be taken away. Food and dignity are rights, so they cannot.

practice.prompt: In a class of {n} children, every child has the right to be heard. How many children have that right?
practice.hint: Do any children have to earn the right first?
practice.explain: All {n} children have it. Rights are universal: every child has them, with no conditions.

choices: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child
pool.hint: It is a promise about the rights of everyone under 18.
pool.explain: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child has 54 articles; 42 of them set out the rights of everyone under 18.

pool.prompt: Can a child lose their right to be safe for breaking a rule?
choices: No, rights cannot be taken away
Yes, if the rule was important
pool.hint: Are rights earned by good behaviour?
pool.explain: Rights are not earned, so they cannot be lost as a punishment. A privilege can be.

pool.prompt: You have the right to say what you think. What is your responsibility?
choices: Let others say what they think too
pool.hint: Everyone has the same right as you.
pool.explain: Because others have the same right, respecting it means listening and taking turns.

pool.prompt: Who has the main duty to provide free schools?
pool.hint: Who builds schools and pays teachers?
pool.explain: Governments are duty bearers: they must make the right to education happen (Article 28).

pool.prompt: Two friends want the same swing. What is a fair fix?
pool.hint: A fair fix keeps both children's right to play.
pool.explain: Taking turns keeps the right to play for both. Grabbing or banning it takes it from someone.

pool.prompt: Mo posts a photo of Lily without asking. Which right is affected?
pool.hint: Lily did not agree to the photo being shared.
pool.explain: Article 16 gives every child a right to privacy, so ask before sharing photos.

pool.prompt: A school takes away {a} minutes of golden time from a child. How many of the child's rights does that remove?
pool.hint: Is golden time a right or a privilege?
pool.explain: The answer is 0. Golden time is a privilege, so removing {a} minutes is allowed and the child keeps every right.

pool.prompt: A charter lists {r} rights. The class writes one way to respect each right. How many ways do they write?
pool.hint: One way for each right on the list.
pool.explain: {r} rights need {r} ways to respect them, one for each.
